prompt: Which lesson of this course asks you to install something, and why that one?
hint: Think about which lesson turns text into pictures.

choices.text: Lesson 1, because each diagram tool has to be set up before the first drawing
choices.why: Paper, diagrams.net or Excalidraw need no setup worth a lesson; the first lessons are about reading and drawing, not tools.

choices.text: Lesson 12, because diagrams written as text need programs that draw them
choices.why: Right: Mermaid, PlantUML and Structurizr turn text into pictures, and lesson 12 sets them up before asking you to type anything.

choices.text: Lesson 5, because decision records need special software to be kept
choices.why: Decision records are plain text files; a folder, ideally in a Git repository, is enough.

choices.text: Lesson 8, because TOGAF is delivered as a modelling tool
choices.why: TOGAF is a published standard, a method and a vocabulary. Tools exist for it, and none is needed to learn it.

prompt: The platform cannot receive a drawing. What do the questions in this course check instead?
hint: One half of the skill can be marked by a machine.

choices.text: The vocabulary of each lesson, with diagrams left aside
choices.why: Many questions show a finished diagram and ask what is wrong with it or what its parts are, which is about diagrams directly.

choices.text: Whether you memorised the figures in each section
choices.why: The questions use new situations as often as the lesson's figures; recalling a picture is not the skill.

choices.text: Reading a diagram critically: naming its parts and finding its faults
choices.why: Yes. Reading is the half a grader can check, and the drawing half is practised on your own against the worked answers.

choices.text: How fast you can draw in an online editor
choices.why: There is no editor in the platform, and speed is not what the course is about.

prompt: What should be written down before a diagram is drawn?
hint: Two lines at the top of the page.

choices.text: The question it answers and the reader who will use it
choices.why: Right: with those two, the scope, the notation and the level of detail mostly decide themselves.

choices.text: The full list of components in the system, so that the picture is complete
choices.why: A full inventory leads to the picture of everything, which answers nothing in particular.

choices.text: The colours and shapes of the company's template
choices.why: A template helps consistency, but it does not tell you what to draw or for whom.

choices.text: The products it uses, so that the right logos can be found and placed
choices.why: Logos say which product is used, not what it does in this system. They are what made the printout on the wall decoration.

prompt: Which of these are signs that a diagram is decoration rather than communication? Choose all that apply.
hint: Decoration makes no claim a reader could check.

choices.text: The same picture is handed to the board, new engineers and auditors
choices.why: Yes: different readers need different answers, so one picture for all serves none of them well.

choices.text: Nothing on it could be contradicted by the running system
choices.why: Yes: a diagram that makes no specific claim cannot be wrong, which also makes it useless as a reference.

choices.text: Product logos carry most of the meaning
choices.why: Yes: a logo names a product, not what that product does here.

choices.text: It leaves out parts of the system that do not bear on its question
choices.why: Leaving things out is what a focused diagram does. The boarding app does not belong on a picture about buying.

prompt: Bento asks where a passenger's CPF is stored. Tainá's diagram for the purchase cannot answer it. What should she do?
hint: One diagram, one question.

choices.text: Add the CPF to each box that touches it, on the purchase diagram
choices.why: That makes one picture answer two questions, and the purchase becomes harder to follow for the reader it was drawn for.

choices.text: Tell him the printout on the wall shows it
choices.why: The printout had two database logos and no way to tell which data was in which; it cannot answer this either.

choices.text: Draw a second picture scoped to where personal data lives
choices.why: Right: a new question gets its own diagram, with only what that question needs.

choices.text: Explain that diagrams are the wrong tool for where data is stored
choices.why: They are not: lesson 3's container diagram names what each database holds.

prompt: An unlabelled arrow runs from the passenger app to the ticketing API. Match each reading to what it would mean.
hint: Each reading is a different claim about the same arrow.

pairs.right: the app sends requests and waits for answers
a change to the API may break the app
the app is owned by or deployed with the API
a step in a process rather than a call

right_distractors: the API decides the colour of the app

prompt: One corner of a diagram uses arrows for calls; another uses them for data flow. What goes wrong for a reader?
hint: A request and its answer travel in opposite directions.

choices.text: Little, as long as the boxes have types
choices.why: Types fix the boxes, not the lines. The arrows still mean two things.

choices.text: Half the arrows point the wrong way for whichever reading they chose
choices.why: Yes: call and data flow can point in opposite directions for one conversation, so a reader who picked one reading misreads the other half.

choices.text: The diagram becomes a sequence diagram
choices.why: A sequence diagram is a specific notation with lifelines and time going down; mixing arrow meanings does not make one.

choices.text: The protocol labels become redundant
choices.why: The protocol says how, not which way the claim runs. The confusion is about direction and meaning.

prompt: By the lesson, what does a good label on a line look like?
hint: It reads in the direction of the arrow.

choices.text: uses
choices.why: It fits every arrow, which is why it tells the reader almost nothing.

choices.text: The name of the team that owns the line, so questions reach somebody
choices.why: Lines are relations between elements; ownership belongs to the elements or to a boundary.

choices.text: A number that points the reader to a table elsewhere in the document
choices.why: That sends the reader away from the page for every line; numbered steps belong to sequences, and even then the step needs words.

choices.text: A verb phrase in the arrow's direction, on every line, with the protocol
choices.why: Right: "sends booking requests to (HTTPS/JSON)" says what and how.

prompt: Celeste, the operations director, wants to know whether a bus can board passengers when the payment provider is down. Which picture serves her?
hint: The right notation is the one the reader can read.

choices.text: A UML sequence diagram of the purchase, with each message drawn
choices.why: Precise and correct, and written in a notation she was never taught. It answers an engineer's question.

choices.text: A class diagram of the booking model
choices.why: It shows structure, not what keeps working when something fails.

choices.text: The printout on the wall
choices.why: It makes no claim about failure at all.

choices.text: A keyed diagram of what boarding needs and what it does without
choices.why: Yes: a light notation with a legend, answering her question in terms she reads.

prompt: On a team's container diagram a dashed line means an asynchronous message. On its deployment diagram, dashed means not built yet. Nothing is wrong on either page alone. What is the problem?
hint: The contract holds across a set of diagrams.

choices.text: A reader who learnt the first meaning misreads the second diagram
choices.why: Right: one meaning per mark across the whole document, or the reader carries the wrong key from one page to the next.

choices.text: Dashed lines are forbidden by the standard notations
choices.why: UML uses dashed lines for several things, such as dependencies and return messages. The problem is the inconsistency, not the dash.

choices.text: Deployment diagrams are not meant to show planned work
choices.why: They can, if the legend says how. Here the trouble is that the same mark means two things in one set.

choices.text: The legend on each page should be removed so readers ask
choices.why: Removing legends makes every mark a guess. The fix is one convention, written once, that every diagram links to.

prompt: Match each term from ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 to its meaning.
hint: The viewpoint is the reusable one.

pairs.right: somebody with an interest in the system
a recipe for a kind of picture
one such picture of one system

right_distractors: the tool used to draw the diagram

prompt: In Kruchten's 4+1 model, what is the +1 for?
hint: It ties the other four together.

choices.text: It is the security view, added in later editions
choices.why: The +1 is the scenarios. Security is a concern that cuts across all the views.

choices.text: It is a summary diagram for executives
choices.why: It is not a summary; it is the set of use cases that checks the others.

choices.text: Checking that the four views agree
choices.why: Yes: a use case walked through each view finds where they disagree or leave a gap.

choices.text: It is the view of the code, generated automatically
choices.why: The code organisation is the development view, one of the four.

prompt: A single diagram shows Carcará's servers, the main classes of the booking model and a numbered timeline of the purchase. Which diagnosis fits?
hint: Count the views on the page.

choices.text: It is fine: one complete picture saves readers time
choices.why: Each reader has to separate the views before reading any of them, which costs more than three smaller pictures.

choices.text: Three views fighting for one page; split it
choices.why: Right: physical, logical and process views, each clearer on its own.

choices.text: It needs a legend, and after that it is correct
choices.why: A legend helps with marks, not with a page answering three different questions.

choices.text: It is the scenarios view, the +1 of Kruchten's model
choices.why: Scenarios are use cases walked through the views, not a merge of the views.

prompt: This is the anatomy diagram from the lesson with its lettering removed. Put each name on the part it belongs to.
hint: The dashed line surrounds things; the arrow joins two of them.

prompt: What is the one check that no checklist replaces?
hint: It needs another person.

choices.text: Re-drawing the diagram in a different tool
choices.why: A new tool changes how it looks, not whether a reader understands it.

choices.text: Counting the elements and keeping under a dozen
choices.why: A useful rule of thumb, and still a check you run on your own.

choices.text: A reader explaining it back to you, unaided
choices.why: Yes: every difference between their explanation and your intent is a mark that made a different claim.

choices.text: Asking the most senior engineer to sign it off
choices.why: Seniority does not make somebody the intended reader, and a signature is not an explanation.

prompt: A diagram is ready when a reader who was not there can answer its ___ from the page alone.
hint: It is written at the top of the page before drawing.

prompt: By the platform's rule, which of these earn a diagram rather than a sentence? Choose all that apply.
hint: Sequence, boundary, count, two axes.

choices.text: The order of the hold, the charge and the confirmation in a purchase
choices.why: Yes: a sequence where later steps depend on earlier ones returning.

choices.text: Which services run in Carcará's account and which belong to the payment company
choices.why: Yes: a boundary, and what crosses it.

choices.text: The ticketing API writes to the booking database
choices.why: That is one sentence; drawn, it is two boxes the reader decodes back into the same sentence.

choices.text: Ticket sales per hour across the week of São João
choices.why: Yes: two axes, where the shape is the argument.

prompt: Why does the lesson say a wrong diagram does more harm than an absent one?
hint: Think about how readers treat a picture.

choices.text: Because readers trust a picture, so a wrong one is believed
choices.why: Right: an absent diagram makes people ask; a wrong one makes them act on it.

choices.text: Because wrong diagrams break the build
choices.why: Most diagrams are not checked by anything, which is exactly why they drift unnoticed.

choices.text: Because auditors fine companies for outdated diagrams
choices.why: That is not the argument; the harm is to the people who read and believe it.

choices.text: Because it takes up space in the repository
choices.why: Storage is cheap. Misleading a reader is not.

prompt: Put the steps of making a diagram for somebody else in a sensible order.
hint: Question first; another person last.
items: Write the question and the reader at the top
Sketch on paper and throw drafts away
Draw only what answers the question, with types and labelled lines
Add the legend, the title and the date
Ask a reader like the intended one to explain it back
trap: Starting from the tool, or from a list of every component, gives the picture of everything.

prompt: Rui shares a whiteboard photo from a design session as the architecture section of a document for the auditors. What is the most accurate criticism?
hint: Who was in the room, and who is reading?

choices.text: Whiteboards are informal, so what is drawn on one is unreliable for an audit
choices.why: Sketching on a whiteboard is valuable. The problem is handing the sketch to people who were not there.

choices.text: Auditors accept UML and refuse other notations
choices.why: There is no such rule; they need a diagram they can read and that answers their question.

choices.text: The photo is too low-resolution to read
choices.why: Even a perfect photo carries the same unexplained marks.

choices.text: It carries private conventions to readers who were not in the room
choices.why: Yes: a sketch is meant to be thrown away or redrawn with a title, types, labels and a legend for its new reader.
